newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Canberra imposes planning laws on telecoms.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Canberra imposes planning laws on telecoms.

text.p: The Australian government said on Tuesday that telecommunications carriers would have to follow state planning laws from July and also make their installations less intrusive between now and then.

"State and territory planning and environmental laws will generally apply to the rollout of telecommunications infrastructure from July 1997 with a few limited exceptions," Communications Minister Richard Alston said in a statement.
"Telecommunications carrier activities have been immune from state and territory laws under the regime inherited from the previous Labor government," he said.
From July carriers would also be required to:
-- Share radiocommunications towers and radiocommunications sites for mobile phone services.
-- Place aerial fibre-optic cabling underground unless permitted by state authorities.
-- Connect new subscribers with underground cable unless the house was on the same side of a street as aerial cabling and the subscriber agrees to aerial connection.
Aerial cabling -- strung from existing power poles -- has generated great hostility from residents groups and local councils, who complain that it is ugly.
For the remainder of the period in which it could be used regardless of state laws, Alston said it would be subject to several new restrictions.
It would have to be grey instead of black, at least 3.5 metres above ground and underground at big intersections.

Councils have also objected to towers for mobile phone services, and Alston said that during the interim period the carriers would have to share them and also consider alternatives proposed by the councils.
The three exceptions to state planning laws that the carriers would still enjoy after July would be:
-- Rights for land inspection, facility maintenance, low impact facility installation, and temporary defence facilities;
-- The establishment of a limited case-by-case appeals process in cases of national significance;
-- Continuation of some particular, but unspecified, powers and immunities under the current act.
Alston said there would be limited transitional arrangements from the current regulatory regime to the new Act.
"Transitionals will apply where an installation has already been through all notification processes and construction has commenced before 1 July 1997," he said.

The transitional period meant that the last broadband aerial cabling would have to be installed by the end of September while other facilities currently immune from the state laws would have to be finished by the end of the year.
